title: Reporting
text: Reporting provides programs the opportunity to link actions to priorities and outcomes.

title: Reporting
text:
Annual Reporting
In Baton Rouge, the open data policy requires annual reporting by the Director of Information Services (Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge 2017).

“The report shall include an assessment of progress toward achievement of the goals of the City-Parish’s Open Data BR program (under which all City-Parish open data related activities occur), an assessment of how the City-Parish’s work has furthered or will further the City-Parish’s programmatic priorities, and a description and publication timeline for datasets envisioned to be published by the City-Parish in the following year.”

Since 2018, they have published annual reports (Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge, n.d.-a), which are often published directly on their open data platform, such as the most recent 2025 Open Data Policy Report (Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge 2025). A consistent feature of their annual reports is the “By the Numbers” section that reports on the number of data products, events, and resulting views and engagement from the community.

title: Reporting
text:
Blogs
Other ways of sharing information about initiatives powered by open data include blog posts. In San Francisco, the new Chief Data Officer explained the strategic vision of the program (Bonaguro 2014) initiated by the updated open data policy (City and County of San Francisco 2013). Civic technology and advocacy organizations in Austin have published advocacy agendas (Open Austin 2016) and contributions through new data, analysis, and advocacy (Carey 2020, 2016; Rosenthal 2013; Open Austin, n.d.).

title: Reporting
text:
Dashboards
Asset inventories available on data portals provide views of all assets, like the Austin Open Data Asset Inventory Dashboard (City of Austin, n.d.). Programs may also add other information to asset inventories like the department assigned value of a dataset, publishing status (some data may only be available internally), update frequency, and monthly views like the San Francisco Dataset Inventory Explorer (City and County of San Francisco, n.d.).
Views of applications that span multiple data platforms can be shown on custom dashboards such as the Transparency Performance Metrics dashboard (Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge, n.d.-b) that includes lifetime views of map applications, web tools, department priority dashboards, and citizen data academy video tutorials.

title: Measuring open data use and public engagement
text:
The open data action toolkit provides guidance on how to measure organizational actions and public engagement with open data. The actions and measures shared in the toolkit were identified from literature review of existing research on open data use and measures, supplemented with findings from case studies of 3 local governments in the United States.
The examples provided in the toolkit are based on the data, data products, and reporting created by case study participants from the City of Austin, the City of Baton Rouge and Parish of East Baton Rouge, and the City and County of San Francisco open data programs. Community developed analysis, tools, and data products are also presented here demonstrating the important role of open data intermediaries to synthesize government data, create innovative tools for exploring data, and advocate on behalf of the public.

Organizational Actions
The toolkit first provides examples of actions taken by organizations to support open data use, through the creation of data products (datasets, maps, applications, dashboards, visualizations, data stories, and initiative websites), providing support, participating in local events, and implementing resolutions, directives, and standards that improve infrastructure and data availability and accessibility.
Learn more about tracking organizational actions that demonstrate the work of creating data products, providing support, participating in events, and issuing policy actions and standards.


Data Portal Measures
The toolkit then demonstrates how to measure direct use of data and other assets published on data portals. Measures include views of datasets, maps, dashboards, visualizations, and data stories. Downloads of data and requests to API (application programming interface) endpoints for datasets are other measures that are available from data portals. Additional context from asset metadata provides another layer of analysis available to evaluate the completeness and usefulness of overall data catalogs.
Learn how to access web analytics from data portals to track public use and evaluate the quality of data catalogs.


Public Engagement Measures
The toolkit also highlight signals of public engagement that include articles published by local news organizations and other community members, attendance at events featuring open data, questions for data owners, support requests, public information requests, engagement with support content, and engaging with council and public advocacy organizations.
Learn more about monitoring public engagement with open data by tracking articles and other public activity.


Reporting
Finally, the toolkit shows how regular reporting enables organizations to link government and community priorities with actions and measures of progress.
Learn how to incorporate reporting requirements and view examples of annual reports, blog posts, analytic dashboards, and a catalog of measures.


Practical Applications
Learn how to apply the toolkit and gain awareness of the open data community in your neighborhood.

title: Articles

Data Methods
The City of San Francisco tracks citations to open data and includes notes about the articles and tools in a spreadsheet. Citation tools, like Zotero, may also be used to organize articles.
The following screenshot of a Power BI report demonstrates the number of articles and blog posts related to open data, data reporting, and events initiating open government transparency between 2009 and 2025. Including notes with links to data sources and newspaper can be used to link articles to data products and provide insights to department data publishers on the use of their data.

title: Articles
text:
Equitable Access to News
While new opportunities for rich storytelling through narratives and digital tools created by data reporters, there is also a concern that they are not accessible to everyone (Felle 2016) and depend on access to devices, internet, and subscriptions to news services.

title: Web Analytics
text:
Web Analytics
Data portals publish the number of page views for data assets on overview pages and through APIs (application programming interface). Tyler Technologies and Esri provide documentation on their use (Tyler Technologies 2022), (Esri, n.d.).

Overview Pages
Dataset overview pages provide important details about the data and lifetime page views and downloads. An example of an overview page is the Issued Construction Permits on the Austin data portal.



Issued Building Permits


In the “About” section, the lifetime views and downloads are shown, which for this dataset consist of 5.38 million views and 82.3 thousand downloads.


APIs (Application programming interfaces)
The Tyler Technologies Discovery API (Socrata Discovery API, n.d.) provides analytic details for all data assets on a data portal that includes lifetime views and downloads, as well as views in the last week and month, providing insights on current public interest. Authentication is not required to access information about published data assets on domain. Tools like Excel and Power BI can easily connect to the API endpoint to make information available for analysis.
Example API endpoint with parameters to retrieve all published data assets by data portal domain:

Austin, Texas

Discovery catalog endpoint: http://api.us.socrata.com/api/catalog/v1?search_context=data.austintexas.gov&published=true&limit=5000

Baton Rouge, Louisiana

Discovery catalog endpoint: http://api.us.socrata.com/api/catalog/v1?search_context=data.brla.gov&published=true&limit=5000

San Francisco, California

Discovery catalog endpoint: http://api.us.socrata.com/api/catalog/v1?search_context=data.sfgov.org&published=true&limit=5000


The following screenshot of a Power BI report demonstrates the type of useful information that can be found about the use of data assets from open data portals. The report and an excel file are available on the code repository for demonstration purposes.



Power BI Report of Discovery API Results

title: Organizational Actions
text: Actions taken to support the use of open data provide indications of commitment by organizations to users.

title: Organizational Actions
text:
Data Products
The creation of new datasets may represent the fulfillment of public requests (Mergel et al. 2018) or signify successful collaboration with departments to publish data that demonstrates their work on behalf of the public (Johnson 2016).
Datasets can be measured by their value to departments and the public. Dataset characteristics like category, agency function, expected user group, information type, and related open government principle have been used to evaluate the public usefulness of a data catalog (Schwoerer 2022). The evaluation of metadata completion, communication mechanisms, and publishing frequency provides a way to track the commitment of a program to providing open data (Nahon et al. 2015).

title: Organizational Actions
text:
Support
Providing users access through support platforms makes it easy to isolate and report open data requests for help, new data, and detailed public information queries. Requests made by the public are valuable opportunities to gather feedback and build trust by responding to matters that are meaningful and personally important to members of the public (Guy 2021).
Online content, communication channels, tutorials, videos, and case studies that enable users are actions that should be reported as organizational action measures.

title: Organizational Actions
text:
Events
Open data day celebrations, datathons, and hackathons are ways that open data programs, departments, community organizations, researchers, local news organizations, and technology sponsors typically engage the public to participate in a day, weekend, or week of using government data to help understand and tackle important community issues.
In addition to counting the number of events and attendees, there are other measures that show the contributions made by the public. Examples of important hackathon measures include new ideas, viable design concepts, prototypes, participant social connections, new start-ups, and increased domain and technical knowledge gains for participants (Jaskiewicz et al. 2019).

title: About
text:
The toolkit identifies the types of measures that signal public use and engagement with open data and provides recommendations for regular reporting of actions and resulting activity.
The development of the open data actions and measures toolkit fulfills one part of a dissertation portfolio that focuses on measuring open data use and engagement to serve and empower the public.

title: Data Catalog Quality
text: To enable the collection of data about actions, programs should consider how they can attach metadata to datasets and data products that explain what initiated its creation and how it supports department and community priorities. and services and priorities. Program should also try to classify other actions like events, enablement content, questions, and support requests within their systems of record so that data can also be shared publicly.

title: Data Catalog Quality
text:
Providing Context
Examples of how to add context to include:

New datasets created through public information requests
New datasets created from actions, resolutions, and directives made by Council, Mayor, or other local government authority
New datasets created from legal settlements.
New datasets created from multiple organizations that share ownership of source data and require coordination.
New datasets created (crowd-sourced) by community members for data not collected by local government organizations.
New datasets initiated from audit recommendations
New datasets initiated from department initiatives
Created to aid emergency response
